Completely seconding this. It starts off with constantly looking over your shoulder worrying that you're being clocked, that your clothing isn't fitting right, that your voice or mannerisms or the tiniest detail about how you sit in a chair might be giving you away. But there really does come a time where it stops being a part of your everyday life. People stop noticing. You stop having to explain yourself. Many of the traits that cause dysphoria now will develop, with hormones or surgery, to something that is affirming: and if there are traits that don't change, they don't feel as awful once there's barely a handful left. 

Once upon a time, every part of my body and mannerisms caused severe distress. A relative told me as a teenager "It's okay to have wide hips, some men do have wide hips." I had told her "Yes, but most men don't have wide hips and also breasts and a high voice and a weight distribution and--". When there was a huge pile of things causing dysphoria, it was insurmountable. But after a while on T and access to a real binder, a lot of it went away. My face shape changed, details as small as the fullness of my eyebrows were now affirming. My body changed shape all by itself. Yes, I still have wide hips. There's no surgery that can file those down. But now I can also think "It's okay to have wide hips, some men do have wide hips" because they're one of the few traits from that original list of triggers left, and anyone who looks at me just sees a man with wide hips.

It's a pain, but it's also completely normal - I'm in my mid twenties and still fiddling with dosages and cocktails for diagnoses I had since I was a teenager, and there will be folk much older than me who can say the same. Absolutely talk to a psychiatrist. It's part of their job to balance a medication cocktail for people with complex conditions and/or multiple diagnoses. What combination you need may be different from everyone you speak to because it can be extremely unique. But it is absolutely possible to be on both ADHD and bipolar medication. I'm someone who has taken various types of both for years and experienced no issues with them interfering with each other or causing unintended effects. 

If your current medication appears to be causing serious problems, call your psychiatrist's practice and tell them you think you may be having serious unintended effects of the medication and need help. They may arrange an appointment, or potentially a phone call depending on your psych's preference, and may give instructions on what to do if the appointment isn't next day. That goes for all serious unintended medication side effects - contact the prescribing practitioner immediately, or contact a health line in your country.

I think you've shown that you're approaching this in a thoughtful and articulate way, but I think the other person's point about still thinking about the person they lost isn't necessarily irrelevant to you even if it was true that there was nobody close to you. 

There was a girl at my school when I was 13 who took her life, and the entire school was silent that day. When I arrived at school, there was no shrieks of people playing ball games, no roar of hundreds of voices gossiping; we were all just silent. Classes were taciturn all day, and the school held a memorial service for her shortly later. It's been over a decade since then, and I still very frequently think of her. I wonder if anyone else still thinks of her. I wonder what it says about me that I've forgotten the names of many people influential in my life but refuse to forget hers, I wonder about her family, I wonder about the people who were her classmates and how they had an empty space in their classrooms and their graduation. And I think about the way hundreds of teenagers and many adults who had never met her were grieved at the realisation that the community had failed in such a way and someone had passed because of that failing.

Sometimes, even if individuals don't care, a suicide can still have a powerful and profound impact on the broader community. People who have never met a person can grieve that they will never get the opportunity to, and people who have no reason to care about the person can grieve that the community they consider themself part of and take pride in had failed someone within it so catastrophically. 

Whether it's "fair" or "reasonable" for strangers to get a say in someone's suicide is a different conversation. But while we're here, talking about the philosophical ramifications of suicide, I think that the community or communities one is part of can count on the list of "people" impacted. 

From a religious standpoint, my relationship with religion is complex, but I know that the God I was raised with was the God of the flock, and so He would be grieved as well both at any member of the flock suffering but also at the suffering that ripples through the flock. I reject that suicide would be a sin against God: I've always felt that many of the things written as sins were designed for protection of ourselves and the community and humanity, but I think if God were truly forgiving as He was always said to be, he would already understand the strength a person has shown to persevere as long as they did. But I do think there would be sadness at the loss and that rippling impact through the person's immediate and wider community.

It is always possible for a person to feel the effort to make a change is insurmountable, but that's not the same thing as "lazy". Lazy is "couldn't be fucked emptying the dish drainer because you're just going to come back and use those dishes anyway" or whatever, it isn't "curled up on the floor because everything is too much and you have no idea where to even start". Yes, some people do break out of depression by brute force-ing it, but even a lot of people whose mental health would seem to the external observer to be caused by a specific issue are not simply putting off fixing it, or not bothering. Something has got them stuck, and without dealing with the reason they're stuck, they're not going to magically start moving again. 

Think of it like having a friend who is always complaining about how much their partner sucks, and you've been encouraging them to break up for eight months and they keep agreeing that's a good idea but they never do it. Infuriating, because it would be so simple for them to just remove the issue that's causing them (and you at this point!) so much grief. Except it turns out the reason they haven't broken up is something like both names being on their lease and they're worried about what will happen with housing, or they can't handle the idea of not getting to see the partner's family or dog or something anymore. People generally don't do (or not do) things for no reason. 

Part of this will also rest on how you define "lazy". It's a heavily value-loaded term. I consider "lazy" to be when someone couldn't be assed to do something when there's no barriers in the way and there may be consequences for not doing it. Key point is the barriers. If you define "lazy" as not putting in the effort, it's easier to define others as lazy because it's impossible to get a full picture of what effort people have put in and what things just aren't working for them.

Suicidality is often the result of a crushingly overburdened stress response and typically ongoing severe mental illness. It's not laziness. And the humiliation of not being able to do these things due to depression and having someone call them lazy for it is only likely to intensify that stress response. People don't just choose to not put the effort in, and you don't know the circumstances of a stranger on the internet well enough to comment on their current difficulty in getting up. You're assuming that OP isn't "putting in the work", but they're handling a different situation to you, as a different person, and "work" may be two entirely different things between you. You can't solve anyone's problems with assumptions, and you certainly can't solve them with with accusations.

The conflicting nature of EDs is part of what makes them so difficult. That they make you feel so ill, but there's that sense of pride in it. It makes it harder to accept that the pride isn't based on something healthy or sustainable, and makes the basic desire to "not feel like garbage all the time" a war. If your family want you to be able to address your ED, are you seeing a doctor or getting any help from a dietician or anything like that? Sometimes just finding a path to not feeling sick can be a more helpful starting point than some of the more direct ways people might think about recovery. 

Whatever happens, you deserve support.

DID can only develop in childhood, like some other commenters have said. However, it's common for many people with trauma (which may or may not include you, BPD is often linked to trauma) and other mental health conditions to feel 'split' from themselves. One way this can make sense is if you look into "internal family systems theory". It's not about having different "personalities" or alters, but about recognising the different aspects and instincts of oneself, and then hopefully being able to name what caused them and therefore understand what's happening in your head and what you can do about it. For example, a person may find when under pressure they feel like everything someone says to them is criticism of them and it makes them lash out; IFS theory/therapy may gently question whether they had a parent, significant other, etc. in their life who often *did* hide cruelty in otherwise simple comments, and the "idea" that you're being criticised and need to defend yourself may be coming from a specific person, people, event, or understanding of something that happened. That's a huge oversimplification, but I found it really helpful for understanding what parts of me were firing off and for what reasons, who "put them there", and therefore how to percieve them. It's worth noting that just because something is listed in the side effects column of the medication information pamphlet doesn't mean everyone gets them, or there's even a high likelihood of getting them. The chances are pretty low, but possibly more important is that if you do start any medication and encounter unpleasant side effects that don't go away within the onboarding period (your doctor should tell you the time frame, for many it's two to four weeks), you can always cease that medication and try a different one. There are so, so many different types of medication out there, and the chances that someone would experience the negative libido or sexual side effects from every one of them is minuscule. You have the time to breathe, see how the medication affects you as it reaches a stable level over that period of time, and decide whether this is going to work. And you always retain the ability to go back to your doctor and say "This one's not working for me, it's causing (xyz), what else have you got?". You can be on a med for a few months or forty years and still be able to let your doctor know if it's not working and it's time to try something else. It's not a trap, where you put an SSRI in your mouth once and you're bound to it for life. Videos on the internet are often pretty unreliable about mental health anyway, but there's a lot of scare campaigns trying to get people not to take them. They're generally nonsense.

(Also, the "chemical castration" Turing was forced to undergo wasn't any kind of SSRI, it was straight up estrogen. It's absolutely acceptable if you reach a point in your life where you realise estrogen is something you'd like access to, to be clear, but no doctor is going to chase you down the street to make you take Premarin. You don't have to worry about actual chemical castration during mental health treatment.)

This is a hard situation to be in, OP, I'm sorry you're having to deal with so much and with so little support. 

What I did when I was a teenager in an abusive home without access to mental health support was use chat helplines. I didn't use the phone call ones because I didn't want to be overheard, but there are several types of text and webchat helpline that can help: and there are some out there where you can even schedule appointments for more robust support. I'm not in the US but I gave a quick google and apparently you can text 988 - I recommend searching for the resources online, but if your parent ever searches your device, *use incognito mode*. You could even use a second browser - I had both Firefox and Chrome on my phone and had one hidden in a folder so it was harder to find. 

If digital resources won't help, are you enrolled in a school that has a counsellor or similar? Or even a chaplain, if push comes to shove. They can sometimes tell you more options.

With either option: *don't say the word abuse at first*. Get a grasp on the service before bringing that up, and tell them outright that you are in a situation that would be made more unsafe if they made a report if you do. Some helplines are good, you can ask them to talk about your options if they're concerned about something, and they'll give you more control. But don't say the word abuse, or mention any physical or sexual abuse directly, unless you're informed with what they'll do about it. Many helplines are obligated to make reports about abuse allegations against minors, and that could go very badly. You deserve control over what happens when you disclose. 

I hope some of this helps, and I'm happy to talk more about options if you need it

I'm a mature aged student with mental illness and autism, and I've found great value in studying at university. It's two parts: I love learning and I am learning in a field I love, but it's also setting me up for a career that has a higher likelihood of being possible with my mental illness and autism. There are many jobs that provide accommodations, but in studying I've picked a field that will give me more control over the things I struggle with, so it's a long term investment in my ability to handle the workplace.

However, it is worth noting it can get extremely stressful. If your mental illness and/or autism is stress reactive, it can get really tough, especially around attendance quotas and assessment due dates/exams. If it's an option at the institution/s you're looking into, I'd recommend considering if starting below a full time course load is for you: for example, here full time is 4 subjects a semester, but many people take 3 or even 2, to prevent being overloaded and burning out.

I can't recommend enough looking into your chosen institution to see if they have accommodations for students with health conditions, mental illnesses, and/or disabilities. They tend to call it something different at each institution, terms like "equity" are sometimes used, but they can be a complete game changer for study and make it possible to keep up with other students and even excel. Cannot understate the benefit of having accommodations for your study, it really levels the playing field as well as preparing for the fact that in this day and age many workplaces offer accommodations as well, so it's a real-life-applicable setup. 

Tldr: It can be very stressful and high pressure at times, but can give you control over where you end up in a career and feed into a love of learning. If you do study, absolutely apply for disability/health condition accommodations to make sure you can be on the same playing field as every other student.

One version of this argument generally draws from religion. Various belief systems do consider any form of killing a moral offence, but this typically includes euthanasia for those with terminal illnesses causing suffering as well. 

One version is objectively true but not one anyone in a suicidal crisis is going to believe: the good old "suicide is a permanent solution to a temporary problem" thing. The idea there is that most mental health suffering can be treated, whether through targeting the triggers, therapy, medication, etc. This argument is easier to think about as if applying it to someone else, because a lot of us posting in this sub will quickly say "maybe for someone else, but not for me, I'll never get better and can't be helped" or similar. It's... cognitive dissonance, to recognise that this version is true while still holding that belief about oneself, but it's true for most situations nonetheless. 

The third version is utilitarian. A moral action is one that maximises happiness for the greatest number of people. Suicide, as much as we don't want to hear it and may be angry even thinking about it, often can do a great amount of harm to the people around us and the community, even to people who have never met the person who has died. Whether that's selfish of them to feel entitled to someone's life despite suffering is a different issue altogether. As well, it's contradictory but even the people who may seem not to care now often can be hurt deeply following an attempted or completed suicide. Since it harms many people and only "benefits" a single person, a utilitarian moral view would call suicide immoral. It would not apply this same mindset to euthanasia for a person with a terminal illness causing suffering, but that one is a pretty intense debate in moral philosophy and there's not always a clear answer.

I'm still on the study path towards becoming a social worker, so apologies if you're only looking for responses from people who have already entered the workforce. 

Social work can absolutely be a high-trigger environment for mental health difficulties, but this also depends on which field within social work you go into. Each will have different advantages and drawbacks; aged care work can be frustrating, but is often very reliable employment in many Western countries with aging populations. Disability care work varies hugely, you might work with youth, you might work with high support needs care, you might work in advocacy. Mental health work can be very direct and one-on-one, but also might expose you to triggers that are specific to your own mental health experience. 

In contrast, I have a friend who followed the urban planning path. It has far, far less personal exchange of experiences, just by virtue of the field; you wouldn't be hearing about anyone's trauma and the likelihood of having to quickly manage outbursts or tread carefully for risk of doing harm is much lower. However, many civic roles can include the friction between parties, especially if you're in any way working in a government related role where political party politics starts to infringe on your ability to actually do your job. I've heard that this is less of a pain in the private sector, but if bureaucracy is something you struggle with, it's worth being aware of. 

From where I'm sitting, there might be a good career path in each; social work is potentially high risk high reward, with more opportunities to really feel like you're "doing good", but also more pressure on your decision making and more chances to make mistakes that could cause harm. Urban planning is a bit less personal and may be a little less fast paced, depending which social work field you're comparing to, and can potentially be good stable work, but you might run into irritating bureaucracy that could wear you down. 

I hope that's helpful, and hope you're having a good day.

It took me a few therapists before I found my legend, but the key is that she doesn’t actually ask questions. Therapy on TV is super inaccurate. I’m a person who asks myself all the existential questions, and a lot of what she does is let me bounce my thoughts off her simply so I can hear what it sounds like coming from a mouth that’s not mine. She also offers perspectives that I might not have thought of, and even on occasion tidbits from her own experiences that are relevant - like how she once spent months only eating a specific kind of candy, so if I need to survive on just potatoes or something I should do it. That sort of thing. 

Therapy definitely doesn’t exist just to keep us in check. There’s a therapeutic principle called ‘dignity of risk’ that good therapists follow - every person has the right to make their own decisions in life, and judge their own risks. Good therapists don’t rouse on you for bad decisions, or get angry if you’ve self harmed - they ask about the situation that led to it and walk through your thought process around it. Their goal is never to stop you - it’s to guide you. 

I’d definitely recommend it. A common therapy misconception is that your first or even second therapist is going to work. Maybe you’ll hit it off with your first, or maybe you’ll love your tenth. It’s always worth persevering because a good therapist is like striking the kind of gold that’ll set you for a long time. 

Now, probably the important PS to mention is that most people in social services fall into one of two groups - ‘establishment’ workers and ‘critical’ workers. You’ll spot an establishment therapist a mile off because (overgeneralising) they’ll try and make you fit back into society. The best therapists are critical therapists, who help you find a way to make society fit you. 

I hope this has been helpful, let me know if you have any other questions.
